chunks.abstract: The Host Driver must configure the Data Timeout Counter Value in the Timeout Control Register (Offset 02Eh) during Host Controller initialization, with the value determined by settings specified in the Capabilities register.
chunks.raw: At the initialization of the Host Controller, the Host Driver shall set the Data Timeout Counter Value according to the Capabilities register.

chunks.abstract: The Timeout Control Register (Offset 02Eh) allows host drivers to configure timeout values exceeding 500ms for SDXC cards, as Physical Layer Specification Version 3.0x permits SDXC cards to indicate 500ms busy states, with flexibility to set longer timeouts regardless of card capacity.
chunks.raw:
Implementation Note:
The Physical Layer Specification Version 3.0x defines that SDXC card may indicate 500ms busy. Then Host Driver may need to change timeout value for SDXC. It is also possible to set more than 500ms timeout regardless of card capacities.

chunks.abstract: The Host Controller samples card interrupt signals during interrupt periods and stores values in a flip-flop; when Card Interrupt Status Enable is cleared to 0, all internal card interrupt signals must be reset.
chunks.raw:
Implementation Note:

The Host Controller may sample the card interrupt signal during interrupt period and may hold its value in the flip-flop. If the Card Interrupt Status Enable is set to 0, the Host Controller shall clear all internal signals regarding Card Interrupt.

chunks.abstract: This register bit controls sampling clock selection for CMD and DAT reception, where 1 indicates successful tuning completion using a tuned clock and 0 indicates fixed clock usage or tuning failure. The bit is set by tuning procedures and can only be cleared to 0, not set to 1, while modification is prohibited during response or data block reception.
chunks.raw:
Host Controller uses this bit to select sampling clock to receive CMD and DAT. This bit is set by tuning procedure and valid after the completion of tuning (when Execute Tuning is cleared). Setting 1 means that tuning is completed successfully and setting 0 means that tuning is failed. Writing 1 to this bit is meaningless and ignored. A tuning circuit is reset by writing to 0. This bit can be cleared with setting Execute Tuning. Once the tuning circuit is reset, it will take time to complete tuning sequence. Therefore, Host Driver should keep this bit to 1 to perform re-tuning sequence to compete re-tuning sequence in a short time. Change of this bit is not allowed while the Host Controller is receiving response or a read data block. Refer to Figure 2-29.

1
Tuned clock is used to sample data
0
Fixed clock is used to sample data

chunks.abstract: The Execute Tuning bit initiates the sampling clock tuning procedure when set to 1 and automatically clears upon completion, with results indicated in the Sampling Clock Select field; writing 0 aborts the procedure.
chunks.raw:
This bit is set to 1 to start tuning procedure and automatically cleared when tuning procedure is completed. The result of tuning is indicated to Sampling Clock Select. Tuning procedure is aborted by writing 0. Refer to Figure 2-29 for more detail about tuning procedure.

1
Execute Tuning
0
Not Tuned or Tuning Completed

chunks.abstract: This register bit controls the Host Controller output driver type selection (A, B, C, or D) for 1.8V signaling operation. The field value is either manually set by the Host Driver or automatically loaded from Preset Value registers, depending on the Preset Value Enable bit setting.
chunks.raw:
Host Controller output driver in 1.8V signaling is selected by this bit. In 3.3V signaling, this field is not effective. This field can be set depends on Driver Type A, C and D support bits in the Capabilities register.

This bit depends on setting of Preset Value Enable.
If Preset Value Enable = 0, this field is set by Host Driver.
If Preset Value Enable = 1, this field is automatically set by a value specified in the one of Preset Value registers.

00b
Driver Type B is Selected (Default)
01b
Driver Type A is Selected
10b
Driver Type C is Selected
11b
Driver Type D is Selected

chunks.abstract: Host Controllers supporting shared bus require duplicated Preset Value register sets for each device at offset 060h-06Fh, which are accessed by selecting the appropriate Clock Pin Select field in the Shared Bus Control register.
chunks.raw: When Host Controller supports shared bus, a set of Preset Value registers for each device is required and the registers location are duplicated to the offset 06Fh-060h. A set of Preset Value registers can be accessible by selecting Clock Pin Select in the Shared Bus Control register.

2.2.16.title: Software Reset Register (Offset 02Fh)

technical_terms: Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error

2.2.16.abstract: This bit indicates the Host Controller's inability to issue Auto CMD12 for stopping memory multiple block data transfers due to errors, rendering other error status bits (D04-D01) meaningless when set to 1; it remains 0 for Auto CMD23-generated errors.

chunks.abstract: This bit indicates the Host Controller's inability to issue Auto CMD12 for stopping memory multiple block data transfers due to errors, rendering other error status bits (D04-D01) meaningless when set to 1; it remains 0 for Auto CMD23-generated errors.
chunks.raw:
If memory multiple block data transfer is not started due to command error, this bit is not set because it is not necessary to issue Auto CMD12. Setting this bit to 1 means the Host Controller cannot issue Auto CMD12 to stop memory multiple block data transfer due to some error. If this bit is set to 1, other error status bits (D04-D01) are meaningless.
This bit is set to 0 when Auto CMD Error is generated by Auto CMD23.

chunks.abstract: This specification defines the Auto CMD Error Status register timing and error detection for three scenarios: issuing Auto CMD12 (checking previous command errors), receiving Auto CMD12 responses (validating response error bits D01-D04), and reading Auto CMD Error Status bit D07 (verifying command issuance capability).
chunks.raw:
The relation between Auto CMD CRC Error and Auto CMD Timeout Error is shown in Table 2-31 :.

The timing of changing Auto CMD Error Status can be classified in three scenarios:

(1) When the Host Controller is going to issue Auto CMD12
Set D00 to 1 if Auto CMD12 cannot be issued due to an error in the previous command.
Set D00 to 0 if Auto CMD12 is issued.
(2) At the end bit of an Auto CMD12 response
Check received responses by checking the error bits D01, D02, D03 and D04.
Set to 1 if error is detected.
Set to 0 if error is not detected.
(3) Before reading the Auto CMD Error Status bit D07
Set D07 to 1 if there is a command cannot be issued
Set D07 to 0 if there is no command to issue

chunks.abstract: The Auto CMD Error Status register generates interrupts when error bits D00-D04 are set, with optimal D07 sampling occurring before reading the register due to asynchronous timing between Auto CMD Error generation and Command register writes; the Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error (D01-D04) does not trigger separate interrupts.
chunks.raw:
Timing of generating the Auto CMD Error and writing to the Command register are asynchronous. Then D07 shall be sampled when driver never writing to the Command register. So just before reading the Auto CMD Error Status register is good timing to set the D07 status bit.

An Auto CMD Error Interrupt is generated when one of the error bits D00 to D04 is set to 1. The Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error does not make any effect on interrupt because it is set when one of bits D01 to D04 is set to 1.

chunks.abstract: The Software Reset Register at offset 02Fh generates a reset pulse when a bit is written to 1, which the Host Controller automatically clears upon completion; the SD Host Driver must verify all bits return to 0 before proceeding.
chunks.raw: A reset pulse is generated when writing 1 to each bit of this register. After completing the reset, the Host Controller shall clear each bit. Because it takes some time to complete software reset, the SD Host Driver shall confirm that these bits are 0.

chunks.abstract: The Software Reset Register (Offset 02Fh) resets the data circuit and DMA circuit, clearing the Buffer Data Port register, specific Present State register bits (Buffer Read/Write Enable, Transfer Active states, DAT Line Active, Command Inhibit), Block Gap Control register fields, and Normal Interrupt Status register flags.
chunks.raw:
Only part of data circuit is reset. DMA circuit is also reset.

The following registers and bits are cleared by this bit:

Buffer Data Port register

Buffer is cleared and initialized.

Present State register

Buffer Read Enable

Buffer Write Enable

Read Transfer Active

Write Transfer Active

DAT Line Active

Command Inhibit (DAT)

Block Gap Control register

Continue Request

Stop At Block Gap Request

Normal Interrupt Status register

Buffer Read Ready

Buffer Write Ready

DMA Interrupt

Block Gap Event

Transfer Complete

2.2.17.title: Normal Interrupt Status Register (Offset 030h)
2.2.17.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Register generates interrupts when enabled status bits are set to 1. Status bits are cleared by writing 1 to RW1C attributes, while ROC attributes remain unchanged. The Card Interrupt clears automatically when the Card Driver services the interrupt condition.

chunks.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Register generates interrupts when enabled status bits are set to 1. Status bits are cleared by writing 1 to RW1C attributes, while ROC attributes remain unchanged. The Card Interrupt clears automatically when the Card Driver services the interrupt condition.
chunks.raw: The Normal Interrupt Status Enable affects reads of this register, but Normal Interrupt Signal Enable does not affect these reads. An interrupt is generated when the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable is enabled and at least one of the status bits is set to 1. Writing 1 to a bit of RW1C attribute clears it; writing 0 keeps the bit unchanged. Writing 1 to a bit of ROC attribute keeps the bit unchanged. More than one status can be cleared with a single register write. The Card Interrupt is cleared when the card stops asserting the interrupt; that is, when the Card Driver services the interrupt condition.

chunks.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Register (Offset 030h) contains a read-only Error Interrupt bit that consolidates all Error Interrupt Status register bits for efficient error checking, and a Re-Tuning Event bit that signals when the Host Driver must perform re-tuning before the next data transfer.
chunks.raw:
Error Interrupt
If any of the bits in the Error Interrupt Status register are set, then this bit is set. Therefore the Host Driver can efficiently test for an error by checking this bit first. This bit is read only.

1
Error
0
No Error

Reserved

Re-Tuning Event
This status is set if Re-Tuning Request in the Present State register changes from 0 to 1. Host Controller requests Host Driver to perform re-tuning for next data transfer. Current data transfer (not large block count) can be completed without re-tuning.

1
Re-Tuning should be performed
0
Re-Tuning is not required

chunks.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Register (Offset 030h) contains status bits for INT_C and INT_B interrupts, which are set when their respective pins are low and enabled. These bits cannot be cleared by writing 1; they require resetting the interrupt factor through the Shared Bus Control register.
chunks.raw:
INT_C
This status is set if INT_C is enabled and INT_C# pin is in low level. Writing this bit to 1 does not clear this bit. It is cleared by resetting the INT_C interrupt factor. Refer to the Shared Bus Control register.

1
INT_C is detected
0
No interrupt is detected

INT_B
This status is set if INT_B is enabled and INT_B# pin is in low level. Writing this bit to 1 does not clear this bit. It is cleared by resetting the INT_B interrupt factor. Refer to the Shared Bus Control register.

1
INT_B is detected
0
No interrupt is detected

2.2.18.title: Error Interrupt Status Register (Offset 032h)
2.2.18.abstract: The Error Interrupt Status Register (Offset 032h) requires both the Error Interrupt Status Enable and Error Interrupt Signal Enable registers to generate interrupts when status bits are set. Status bits are write-1-to-clear, write-0-to-preserve, with support for clearing multiple bits in a single write operation.

chunks.abstract: The Error Interrupt Status Register (Offset 032h) requires both the Error Interrupt Status Enable and Error Interrupt Signal Enable registers to generate interrupts when status bits are set. Status bits are write-1-to-clear, write-0-to-preserve, with support for clearing multiple bits in a single write operation.
chunks.raw: Signals defined in this register can be enabled by the Error Interrupt Status Enable register, but not by the Error Interrupt Signal Enable register. The interrupt is generated when the Error Interrupt Signal Enable is enabled and at least one of the statuses is set to 1. Writing to 1 clears the bit and writing to 0 keeps the bit unchanged. More than one status can be cleared at the one register write.

chunks.abstract: The Error Interrupt Status Register (Offset 032h) defines error status bits, including vendor-specific fields and a Tuning Error bit that indicates unrecoverable tuning circuit errors outside tuning procedures, requiring command abortion, data transfer retry, and resetting the sampling clock to 0.
chunks.raw:
Vendor Specific Error Status

Additional status bits can be defined in this register by the vendor.

Reserved

Tuning Error

This bit is set when an unrecoverable error is detected in a tuning circuit except during tuning procedure (Occurrence of an error during tuning procedure is indicated by Sampling Select). By detecting Tuning Error, Host Driver needs to abort a command executing and perform tuning. To reset tuning circuit, Sampling Clock shall be set to 0 before executing tuning procedure (Refer to Figure 2-29). The Tuning Error is higher priority than the other error interrupts generated during data transfer. By detecting Tuning Error, the Host Driver should discard data transferred by a current read/write command and retry data transfer after the Host Controller retrieved from tuning circuit error.

1 Error
0 No Error

chunks.abstract: The ADMA Error bit in the Error Interrupt Status Register (Offset 032h) indicates errors during ADMA data transfer, with error states saved in the ADMA Error Status Register. It triggers when invalid descriptor data (Valid=0) is detected at ST_FDS state, allowing the Host Driver to identify the error descriptor.
chunks.raw:
ADMA Error

This bit is set when the Host Controller detects errors during ADMA based data transfer. The state of the ADMA at an error occurrence is saved in the ADMA Error Status Register,

In addition, the Host Controller generates this Interrupt when it detects invalid descriptor data (Valid=0) at the ST_FDS state. ADMA Error State in the ADMA Error Status indicates that an error occurs in ST_FDS state. The Host Driver may find that Valid bit is not set at the error descriptor.

1 Error
0 No Error

chunks.abstract: This field selects one of seven available clock pin outputs (CLK[1] through CLK[7]) or disables clock pins entirely (000b), with selection of unsupported pins having no effect; timing specifications are detailed in Figure 2-38.
chunks.raw:
One of clock pin outputs is selected by this field. Select of unsupported clock pin is meaningless. Refer to Figure 2-38 for the timing of clock outputs.

000b Clock Pins are Disabled
001b CLK[1] is Selected
010b CLK[2] is Selected
...... ..........
111b CLK[7] is Selected

chunks.abstract: This register configures bus width (4-bit or 8-bit) for up to 7 embedded devices on a shared bus configuration, with bits D24-D30 individually controlling each device's data transfer width when Slot Type is set to 10b in the Capabilities register.
chunks.raw:
Shared bus supports mixing of 4-bit and 8-bit bus width devices. Each bit of this field specifies the bus width for each embedded device. The number of devices supported is specified by Number of Clock Pins and a maximum of 7 devices are supported. This field is effective when multiple devices are connected to a shared bus (Slot Type is set to 10b in the Capabilities register). In the other case, Extended Data Transfer Width in the Host Control 1 register is used to select 8-bit bus width. As use of 1-bit mode is not intended for shared bus, Data Transfer Width in the Host Control 1 register should be set to 1.

D24 Bus Width Preset for Device 1
D25 Bus Width Preset for Device 2
D26 Bus Width Preset for Device 3
D27 Bus Width Preset for Device 4
D28 Bus Width Preset for Device 5
D29 Bus Width Preset for Device 6
D30 Bus Width Preset for Device 7

The function of each bit is defined as follows:
0 4-bit bus width mode (Data Transfer Width = 1)
1 8-bit bus width mode

chunks.abstract: This Error Interrupt Status Register field defines support for three asynchronous, open-drain interrupt input pins (INT_A#, INT_B#, INT_C#) in shared bus systems, with a 2-bit encoding indicating whether no interrupts, only INTA, INTA+INTB, or all three interrupt pins are supported.
chunks.raw:
This field indicates support of interrupt input pins for shared bus system. Three asynchronous interrupt pins are defined, INT_A#, INT_B# and INT_C#. Which interrupt pin is used is determined by the system. Each one is driven by open drain and then wired or connection is possible.

00b Interrupt Input Pin is Not Supported
01b INTA is Supported
10b INTA and INTB are Supported
11b INTA, INTB and INTC are Supported

2.2.19.title: Normal Interrupt Status Enable Register (Offset 034h)
2.2.19.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Enable Register at offset 034h controls interrupt status reporting by enabling individual interrupt sources when their corresponding bits are set to 1.

chunks.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Enable Register at offset 034h controls interrupt status reporting by enabling individual interrupt sources when their corresponding bits are set to 1.
chunks.raw: Setting to 1 enables Interrupt Status.

chunks.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Enable Register (Offset 034h) allows the Host Driver to control error interrupts and manage re-tuning events and INT_C status, where clearing the INT_C Status Enable bit forces the Host Controller to clear system interrupt requests.
chunks.raw:
The Host Driver shall control error interrupts using the Error Interrupt Status Enable register.

Re-Tuning Event Status Enable

1
Enabled
0
Masked

INT_C Status Enable
If this bit is set to 0, the Host Controller shall clear the interrupt request to the System. The Host Driver may clear this bit before servicing the INT_C and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests to INT_C pin are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.

1
Enabled
0
Masked

chunks.abstract: The Normal Interrupt Status Enable Register (Offset 034h) controls INT_A and INT_B interrupt requests to the system, where setting bits to 0 masks interrupts and 1 enables them. Host drivers can toggle these bits during interrupt servicing to prevent inadvertent interrupt generation.
chunks.raw:
INT_B Status Enable
If this bit is set to 0, the Host Controller shall clear the interrupt request to the System. The Host Driver may clear this bit before servicing the INT_B and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests to INT_B pin are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.

1
Enabled
0
Masked

INT_A Status Enable
If this bit is set to 0, the Host Controller shall clear the interrupt request to the System. The Host Driver may clear this bit before servicing the INT_A and may set this bit again after all interrupt requests to INT_A pin are cleared to prevent inadvertent interrupts.

1
Enabled
0
Masked

2.2.20.title: Error Interrupt Status Enable Register (Offset 036h)
2.2.20.abstract: The Error Interrupt Status Enable Register at offset 036h controls interrupt status reporting by enabling interrupts when set to 1.

chunks.abstract: The Error Interrupt Status Enable Register at offset 036h controls interrupt status reporting by enabling interrupts when set to 1.
chunks.raw: Setting to 1 enables Interrupt Status.

2.2.21.title: Normal Interrupt Signal Enable Register (Offset 038h)
2.2.21.abstract: This register enables selective interrupt generation by allowing individual interrupt status bits to be set to 1, determining which status conditions trigger the shared interrupt line to the Host System.

chunks.abstract: This register enables selective interrupt generation by allowing individual interrupt status bits to be set to 1, determining which status conditions trigger the shared interrupt line to the Host System.
chunks.raw: This register is used to select which interrupt status is indicated to the Host System as the interrupt. These status bits all share the same1 bit interrupt line. Setting any of these bits to 1 enables interrupt generation.

2.2.22.title: Error Interrupt Signal Enable Register (Offset 03Ah)
2.2.22.abstract: This register enables interrupt generation by selecting which error interrupt status conditions are reported to the Host System via a shared single-bit interrupt line, where setting individual bits to 1 activates the corresponding interrupt notification.

chunks.abstract: This register enables interrupt generation by selecting which error interrupt status conditions are reported to the Host System via a shared single-bit interrupt line, where setting individual bits to 1 activates the corresponding interrupt notification.
chunks.raw: This register is used to select which interrupt status is notified to the Host System as the interrupt. These status bits all share the same 1 bit interrupt line. Setting any of these bits to 1 enables interrupt generation.

2.2.23.title: Auto CMD Error Status Register (Offset 03Ch)

technical_terms: Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error

2.2.23.abstract: This register indicates response errors for Auto CMD12 and Auto CMD23 commands at offset 03Ch, with Auto CMD23 errors specifically mapped to bits 04-01, enabling the host driver to identify specific error types when Auto CMD Error flag is set.

chunks.abstract: This register indicates response errors for Auto CMD12 and Auto CMD23 commands at offset 03Ch, with Auto CMD23 errors specifically mapped to bits 04-01, enabling the host driver to identify specific error types when Auto CMD Error flag is set.
chunks.raw: This register is used to indicate CMD12 response error of Auto CMD12 and CMD23 response error of Auto CMD23. The Host driver can determine what kind of Auto CMD12 / CMD23 errors occur by this register. Auto CMD23 errors are indicated in bit 04-01.This register is valid only when the Auto CMD Error is set.

chunks.abstract: This register reports Auto CMD12/CMD23 error conditions, including command timeout (no response within 64 SDCLK cycles), CRC errors, end bit errors, index errors, and command execution failures, with timeout errors taking precedence over other error status indicators.
chunks.raw:
Command Not Issued By Auto CMD12 Error
Setting this bit to 1 means CMD_wo_DAT is not executed due to an Auto CMD12 Error (D04-D01) in this register.
This bit is set to 0 when Auto CMD Error is generated by Auto CMD23.

Auto CMD Index Error

This bit is set if the Command Index error occurs in response to a command.

Auto CMD End Bit Error

This bit is set when detecting that the end bit of command response is 0.

Auto CMD CRC Error
This bit is set when detecting a CRC error in the command response.

Auto CMD Timeout Error
This bit is set if no response is returned within 64 SDCLK cycles from the end bit of command.
If this bit is set to1, the other error status bits (D04-D02) are meaningless.

2.2.24.title: Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh)
2.2.24.abstract: The Write Transfer Active status bit (bit 08) in the Host Control 2 Register indicates whether a write data transfer is currently active in the Host Controller, being set after a write command's end bit and cleared after receiving CRC status of the final data block.

chunks.abstract: The Write Transfer Active status bit (bit 08) in the Host Control 2 Register indicates whether a write data transfer is currently active in the Host Controller, being set after a write command's end bit and cleared after receiving CRC status of the final data block.
chunks.raw:
08 ROC Write Transfer Active
This status indicates a write transfer is active. If this bit is 0, it means no valid write data exists in the Host Controller. Refer to Section 3.12.4 for more details on the sequence of events.

This bit is set in either of the following cases:
(1) After the end bit of the write command.
(2) When write operation is restarted by writing a 1 to Continue Request in the Block Gap Control register.
This bit is cleared in either of the following cases:
(1) After getting the CRC status of the last data block as specified by the transfer count (Single and Multiple) In case of ADMA2, transfer count is designated by Descriptor Table.
(2) After getting the CRC status of any block where data transmission is about to be stopped by a Stop At Block Gap Request.

During a write transaction, a Block Gap Event interrupt is generated when this bit is changed to 0, as the result of the Stop At Block Gap Request being set. This status is useful for the Host Driver in determining non DAT line commands can be issued during write busy.

1 Transferring data
0 No valid data

chunks.abstract: The Host Control 2 Register at offset 03Eh contains reserved bits in positions 07-04, with no defined functionality assigned to these bit fields.
chunks.raw: 07-04 Rsvd Reserved

chunks.abstract: The Re-Tuning Request bit (ROC) enables the Host Controller to signal the Host Driver to re-execute the tuning sequence when temperature drift shifts the data window, requiring sampling point recalibration; this bit auto-clears when Execute Tuning is set and only functions when using variable sampling clock mode.
chunks.raw:
03 ROC Re-Tuning Request
Host Controller may request Host Driver to execute re-tuning sequence by setting this bit when the data window is shifted by temperature drift and a tuned sampling point does not have a good margin to receive correct data.
This bit is cleared when a command is issued with setting Execute Tuning in the Host Control 2 register.
Changing of this bit from 0 to 1 generates Re-Tuning Event. Refer to Normal Interrupt Status registers for more detail.
This bit isn't set to 1 if Sampling Clock Select in the Host Control 2 register is set to 0 (using fixed sampling clock). Refer to Re-Tuning Modes in the Capabilities register for more detail.

1 Sampling clock needs re-tuning
0 Fixed or well tuned sampling clock

chunks.abstract: The DAT Line Active bit (Offset 03Eh, bit 02) indicates active data transfers on the SD Bus, setting after read command end bits or continue requests, and clearing when transfers complete or block gap stops occur, generating Block Gap Event interrupts when transitioning from 1 to 0.
chunks.raw:
02 ROC DAT Line Active
This bit indicates whether one of the DAT line on SD Bus is in use.

(a) In the case of read transactions
This status indicates whether a read transfer is executing on the SD Bus. Changing this value from 1 to 0 generates a Block Gap Event interrupt in the Normal Interrupt Status register, as the result of the Stop At Block Gap Request being set. Refer to Section 3.12.3 for details on timing.

This bit shall be set in either of the following cases:
(1) After the end bit of the read command.
(2) When writing a 1 to Continue Request in the Block Gap Control register to restart a read transfer.
This bit shall be cleared in either of the following cases:

chunks.abstract: The Buffer Read Enable flag is a read-only status bit in the Host Control 2 Register that indicates when valid data exists in the host-side buffer for non-DMA read transfers, transitioning from 0 to 1 when block data becomes available and generating a Buffer Read Ready interrupt.
chunks.raw:
Buffer Read Enable
This status is used for non-DMA read transfers.
The Host Controller may implement multiple buffers to transfer data efficiently. This read only flag indicates that valid data exists in the host side buffer. If this bit is 1, readable data exists in the buffer. A change of this bit from 1 to 0 occurs when all the block data is read from the buffer. A change of this bit from 0 to 1 occurs when block data is ready in the buffer and generates the Buffer Read Ready interrupt.

chunks.abstract: The Buffer Write Enable is a read-only status flag in the Host Control 2 Register that indicates buffer availability for non-DMA write transfers, transitioning from 1 to 0 when block data is fully written and from 0 to 1 when new buffer space becomes available, triggering a Buffer Write Ready interrupt.
chunks.raw:
Buffer Write Enable
This status is used for non-DMA write transfers.
The Host Controller can implement multiple buffers to transfer data efficiently. This read only flag indicates if space is available for write data. If this bit is 1, data can be written to the buffer. A change of this bit from 1 to 0 occurs when all the block data is written to the buffer. A change of this bit from 0 to 1 occurs when top of block data can be written to the buffer and generates the Buffer Write Ready interrupt. The Host Controller should neither set Buffer Write Enable nor generate Buffer Write Ready Interrupt after the last block data is written to the Buffer Data Port Register.

chunks.abstract: The Read Transfer Active bit in the Host Control 2 Register indicates ongoing read transfer status, setting to 1 after read command completion or restart, and clearing to 0 when data transfer completes via block length specification, ADMA2 descriptor, or block gap request, triggering a Transfer Complete interrupt.
chunks.raw:
Read Transfer Active
This status is used for detecting completion of a read transfer. Refer to Section 3.12.3 for sequence details.

This bit is set to 1 for either of the following conditions:
(1) After the end bit of the read command.
(2) When read operation is restarted by writing a 1 to Continue Request in the Block Gap Control register.

This bit is cleared to 0 for either of the following conditions::
(1) When the last data block as specified by block length is transferred to the System.
(2) In case of ADMA2, end of read operation is designated by Descriptor Table.
(3) When all valid data blocks in the Host Controller have been transferred to the System and no current block transfers are being sent as a result of the Stop At Block Gap Request being set to 1.

A Transfer Complete interrupt is generated when this bit changes to 0.

chunks.abstract: The Preset Value Enable bit in Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) controls whether SDCLK frequency and driver strength are automatically selected by the Host Controller using Preset Value registers (bit=1) or manually configured by the Host Driver through Clock Control and Host Control 2 registers (bit=0).
chunks.raw:
Host Controller Version 3.00 supports this bit.
As the operating SDCLK frequency and I/O driver strength depend on the Host System implementation, it is difficult to determine these parameters in the Standard Host Driver. When Preset Value Enable is set, automatic SDCLK frequency generation and driver strength selection is performed without considering system specific conditions. This bit enables the functions defined in the Preset Value registers.

1
Automatic Selection by Preset Value are Enabled
0
SDCLK and Driver Strength are controlled by Host Driver

If this bit is set to 0, SDCLK Frequency Select, Clock Generator Select in the Clock Control register and Driver Strength Select in Host Control 2 register are set by Host Driver.
If this bit is set to 1, SDCLK Frequency Select, Clock Generator Select in the Clock Control register and Driver Strength Select in Host Control 2 register are set by Host Controller as specified in the Preset Value registers.

chunks.abstract: This register bit enables asynchronous interrupt support in 4-bit SD mode, allowing the host driver to stop SDCLK during interrupt periods for power savings while the host controller continues to deliver card interrupts when the card supports asynchronous interrupts and DAT[1] interrupt is used.
chunks.raw:
This bit can be set to 1 if a card supports asynchronous interrupts and Asynchronous Interrupt Support is set to 1 in the Capabilities register. Asynchronous interrupt is effective when DAT[1] interrupt is used in 4-bit SD mode (and zero is set to Interrupt Pin Select in the Shared Bus Control register). If this bit is set to 1, the Host Driver can stop the SDCLK during asynchronous interrupt period to save power. During this period, the Host Controller continues to deliver the Card Interrupt to the host when it is asserted by the Card.

1
Enabled
0
Disabled

chunks.abstract: The Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) configures slot voltage: removable card slots (Type 00b) default to 3.3V or fall back to 3.0V, while embedded device slots (Type 01b/11b) select one supported voltage bit for the VDDH host interface.
chunks.raw:
If a slot is for removable card (Slot Type = 00b), Host System can set Voltage Support 3.3V or 3.0V. Host Driver selects 3.3V in default. If 3.3V is not supported, 3.0V is selected.

If a slot is for embedded device (Slot Type = 01b or 11b), Host System can set one of Voltage Support bits for host interface voltage (VDDH).

chunks.abstract: The Host Control 2 Register (Offset 03Eh) specifies the SD Clock's base frequency using either 6-bit mode (10-63MHz for versions 1.00/2.00) or 8-bit mode (10-255MHz for version 3.00), with 1MHz units. The Host Driver uses this value to calculate clock divider settings while ensuring frequency limits are not exceeded.
chunks.raw:
This value indicates the base (maximum) clock frequency for the SD Clock. Definition of this field depends on Host Controller Version.

(1) 6-bit Base Clock Frequency
This mode is supported by the Host Controller Version 1.00 and 2.00. Upper 2 bits are not effective and always 0. Unit values are 1MHz. The supported clock range is 10MHz to 63MHz.

(2) 8-bit Base Clock Frequency
This mode is supported by the Host Controller Version 3.00. Unit values are 1MHz. The supported clock range is 10MHz to 255MHz.

If the real frequency is 16.5MHz, the lager value shall be set 0001 0001b (17MHz) because the Host Driver use this value to calculate the clock divider value (Refer to the SDCLK Frequency Select in the Clock Control register.) and it shall not exceed upper limit of the SD Clock frequency. If these bits are all 0, the Host System has to get information via another method.

chunks.abstract: This register bit indicates the time unit of the base clock frequency utilized for detecting Data Timeout Errors in the host controller.
chunks.raw: This bit shows the unit of base clock frequency used to detect Data Timeout Error.

chunks.abstract: The Host Control 2 Register's Timeout Clock Frequency field specifies the base clock frequency (1-63 KHz or 1-63 MHz) used for Data Timeout Error detection, with units determined by the Timeout Clock Unit bit setting.
chunks.raw: This bit shows the base clock frequency used to detect Data Timeout Error. The Timeout Clock Unit defines the unit of this field's value. Timeout Clock Unit =0 [KHz] unit: 1KHz to 63KHz Timeout Clock Unit =1 [MHz] unit: 1MHz to 63MHz

2.2.25.title: Capabilities Register (Offset 040h)
2.2.25.abstract: The Capabilities Register at offset 040h provides host controller implementation-specific information to the Host Driver, with values either fixed or loaded from flash memory during power-on initialization, as controlled by the Software Reset register's All function.

chunks.abstract: The Capabilities Register at offset 040h provides host controller implementation-specific information to the Host Driver, with values either fixed or loaded from flash memory during power-on initialization, as controlled by the Software Reset register's All function.

The Host Controller may implement these values as fixed or loaded from flash memory during power on initialization. Refer to Software Reset For All in the Software Reset register for loading from flash memory and completion timing control.

2.2.26.title: Maximum Current Capabilities Register (Offset 048h)
2.2.26.abstract: The Maximum Current Capabilities Register (Offset 048h) specifies the maximum current available for each supported voltage level, with values valid only when Voltage Support is enabled in the Capabilities register; registers default to 0 if the Host System provides this information through alternative methods.

chunks.abstract: The Maximum Current Capabilities Register (Offset 048h) specifies the maximum current available for each supported voltage level, with values valid only when Voltage Support is enabled in the Capabilities register; registers default to 0 if the Host System provides this information through alternative methods.
chunks.raw: These registers indicate maximum current capability for each voltage. The value is meaningful if Voltage Support is set in the Capabilities register. If this information is supplied by the Host System via another method, all Maximum Current Capabilities register shall be 0.

chunks.abstract: The Maximum Current Capabilities Register at offset 048h measures current in 4mA increments and uses Table 2-36 to specify current support levels for each voltage level.
chunks.raw: This register measures current in 4mA steps. Each voltage level's current support is described using the Table 2-36.

chunks.abstract: The Maximum Current Capabilities Register (Offset 048h) enables SDXC Host Drivers to set the XPC bit in ACMD41 based on power supply capacity: XPC=1 for systems supporting >150mA, XPC=0 for systems supporting <150mA, per Physical Layer Specification v3.0x.
chunks.raw: SDXC card supported Host Driver needs to check this register to determine XPC value in the argument of ACMD41. If a Host System can afford more than 150mA, Host Driver set XPC to 1. If a Host System can afford less than 150mA, Host Driver set XPC to 0. Refer to the Physical Layer Specification Version 3.0x for more detail of XPC.

2.2.27.title: Force Event Register for Auto CMD Error Status (Offset 050h)
2.2.27.abstract: The Force Event Register for Auto CMD Error Status (Offset 050h) requires Host Driver to enable both Command Timeout Error Status and Command CRC Error Status bits to detect CMD line conflicts during automatic command execution.

chunks.abstract: The Force Event Register for Auto CMD Error Status (Offset 050h) requires Host Driver to enable both Command Timeout Error Status and Command CRC Error Status bits to detect CMD line conflicts during automatic command execution.
chunks.raw: Implementation Note: To detect CMD line conflict, the Host Driver must set both Command Timeout Error Status Enable and Command CRC Error Status Enable to 1.

chunks.abstract: The Force Event Register (Offset 050h) is a non-physical write-only address that allows software to set bits in the Auto CMD Error Status Register by writing 1 (writing 0 has no effect), enabling error condition testing and debugging.
chunks.raw:
The Force Event Register is not a physically implemented register. Rather, it is an address at which the Auto CMD Error Status Register can be written.
 Writing 1 : set each bit of the Auto CMD Error Status Register
 Writing 0 : no effect

2.2.28.title: Force Event Register for Error Interrupt Status (Offset 052h)
2.2.28.abstract: The Force Event Register for Error Interrupt Status (Offset 052h) controls software reset for the CMD line, which partially resets the command circuit by clearing the Command Inhibit (CMD) bit in the Present State register and the Command Complete bit in the Normal Interrupt Status register.

chunks.abstract: The Force Event Register for Error Interrupt Status (Offset 052h) controls software reset for the CMD line, which partially resets the command circuit by clearing the Command Inhibit (CMD) bit in the Present State register and the Command Complete bit in the Normal Interrupt Status register.

chunks.abstract: The Software Reset For All bit resets the entire Host Controller except card detection, clearing ROC/RW/RW1C/RWAC register bits to 0. The Host Controller clears this bit when Capabilities registers become valid for reading; if set to 1, the host driver must issue a reset command and reinitialize the SD card.
chunks.raw:
RWAC Software Reset For All
This reset affects the entire Host Controller except for the card detection circuit. Register bits of type ROC, RW, RW1C, RWAC are cleared to 0. During its initialization, the Host Driver shall set this bit to 1 to reset the Host Controller. The Host Controller shall reset this bit to 0 when Capabilities registers are valid and the Host Driver can read them. Additional use of Software Reset For All may not affect the value of the Capabilities registers. If this bit is set to 1, the host driver should issue reset command and reinitialize the SD card.

chunks.abstract: The Force Event Register at offset 052h is a virtual write-only address that sets bits in the Error Interrupt Status Register when corresponding Error Interrupt Status Enable bits are set, allowing software to trigger error interrupts for testing purposes (requires both Status Enable and Signal Enable to generate actual interrupt signals).
chunks.raw:
The Force Event Register is not a physically implemented register. Rather, it is an address at which the Error Interrupt Status register can be written. The effect of a write to this address will be reflected in the Error Interrupt Status Register if the corresponding bit of the Error Interrupt Status Enable Register is set.
 Writing 1 : set each bit of the Error Interrupt Status Register
 Writing 0 : no effect

Note: By setting this register, the Error Interrupt can be set in the Error Interrupt Status register. In order to generate interrupt signal, both the Error Interrupt Status Enable and Error Interrupt Signal Enable shall be set.

2.2.29.title: ADMA Error Status Register (Offset 054h)
2.2.29.abstract: The ADMA Error Status Register captures the ADMA state machine status when an error interrupt occurs, storing the state in the ADMA Error States field while the ADMA System Address Register holds the address near the error descriptor, enabling the host driver to identify and recover from the specific error location.

chunks.abstract: The ADMA Error Status Register captures the ADMA state machine status when an error interrupt occurs, storing the state in the ADMA Error States field while the ADMA System Address Register holds the address near the error descriptor, enabling the host driver to identify and recover from the specific error location.
chunks.raw:
When ADMA Error Interrupt is occurred, the ADMA Error States field in this register holds the ADMA state and the ADMA System Address Register holds the address around the error descriptor. For recovering the error, the Host Driver requires the ADMA state to identify the error descriptor address as follows:

ST_STOP: Previous location set in the ADMA System Address register is the error descriptor address
ST_FDS: Current location set in the ADMA System Address register is the error descriptor address
ST_CADR: This sate is never set because do not generate ADMA error in this state.
ST_TFR: Previous location set in the ADMA System Address register is the error descriptor address

chunks.abstract: The ADMA Error Status Register (Offset 054h) specifies that hosts must use ACMD22 for write block verification due to potential unwritten data in the controller, and documents that ADMA Error Interrupts occur when invalid descriptors (Valid=0) are detected at ST_FDS state, allowing driver identification of invalid descriptors.
chunks.raw:
In case of write operation, the Host Driver should use ACMD22 to get the number of written block rather than using this information, since unwritten data may exist in the Host Controller.
The Host Controller generates the ADMA Error Interrupt when it detects invalid descriptor data (Valid=0) at the ST_FDS state. In this case, ADMA Error State indicates that an error occurs at ST_FDS state. The Host Driver may find that the Valid bit is not set in the error descriptor.

2.2.30.title: ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h)
2.2.30.abstract: The ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) stores the physical memory address of the descriptor table used by the Advanced DMA controller to perform data transfers between system memory and the host controller.

chunks.abstract: The ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) stores the physical memory address of the descriptor table used by the Advanced DMA controller to perform data transfers between system memory and the host controller.
chunks.raw: This register contains the physical Descriptor address used for ADMA data transfer.

chunks.abstract: The ADMA System Address Register (Offset 058h) holds the byte address of the executing command in the Descriptor table, which must be programmed on 32-bit boundaries by the Host Driver. ADMA2 automatically increments this address when fetching descriptor lines and ignores the lower 2 bits, assuming them to be 00b.
chunks.raw: This register holds byte address of executing command of the Descriptor table. 32-bit Address Descriptor uses lower 32-bit of this register. At the start of ADMA, the Host Driver shall set start address of the Descriptor table. The ADMA increments this register address, which points to next line, when every fetching a Descriptor line. When the ADMA Error Interrupt is generated, this register shall hold valid Descriptor address depending on the ADMA state. The Host Driver shall program Descriptor Table on 32-bit boundary and set 32-bit boundary address to this register. ADMA2 ignores lower 2-bit of this register and assumes it to be 00b.

2.2.31.title: Preset Value Registers (Offset 06F-060h)
2.2.31.abstract: Preset Value Registers (offset 06F-060h) automatically configure SDCLK frequency, clock generator, and driver strength settings based on selected bus speed mode when Preset Value Enable is set. During initialization, the host driver must manually configure the clock preset value before enabling automatic preset functionality.

chunks.abstract: Preset Value Registers (offset 06F-060h) automatically configure SDCLK frequency, clock generator, and driver strength settings based on selected bus speed mode when Preset Value Enable is set. During initialization, the host driver must manually configure the clock preset value before enabling automatic preset functionality.
chunks.raw: Table 2-41 shows a set of preset values per card or device. One of the Preset Value registers (06Eh - 062h) is effective based on the Selected Bus Speed Mode. Table 2-42 defines the conditions to select one of Preset Value registers and Figure 2-36 defines fields of a Preset Value register. When Preset Value Enable in the Host Control 2 Register is set to 1, SDCLK Frequency Select and Clock Generator Select in the Clock Control Register, and Driver Strength Select in the Host Control 2 Register are automatically set based on the Selected Bus Speed Mode. This means the Host Driver needs not set these fields when preset is enabled. A Preset Value for Initialization (060h) is not selected by bus speed mode. Before starting the initialization sequence, the Host Driver needs to set a clock preset value to SDCLK Frequency Select in the Clock Control Register. Preset Value Enable can be set after initialization completed.

2.2.32.title: Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h)
2.2.32.abstract: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) is an optional register whose devices require host system-specific drivers rather than Standard Host Driver control, as shared bus configuration is host system-dependent.

chunks.abstract: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) is an optional register whose devices require host system-specific drivers rather than Standard Host Driver control, as shared bus configuration is host system-dependent.
chunks.raw: This register is optional. The devices on shared bus are not intended to be controlled by the Standard Host Driver. This is because shared bus configuration depends on a host system; the devices on shared bus may be controlled by a specific driver of a host system.

chunks.abstract: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) manages back-end power supply for up to 7 embedded devices through individual bit controls (D16-D22), independent of host interface voltage (VDDH). Power control is effective for memory devices in Sleep State supporting CMD14 and SDIO devices when IOEx is disabled.
chunks.raw:
Back-End Power Control

Each bit of this field controls back-end power supply for an embedded device. Host interface voltage (VDDH) is not controlled by this field. The number of devices supported is specified by Number of Clock Pins and a maximum of 7 devices can be controlled.

Back-End power control is effective for embedded memory devices in the Sleep State that support the Sleep command (CMD14) to reduce power consumption and embedded SDIO devices when IOEx is set to 0.

chunks.abstract: The Shared Bus Control Register (Offset 0E0h) Interrupt Pin Select field enables interrupt pin inputs through bit-coded values, where bits enable INT_A, INT_B, and INT_C respectively, with 000b designating interrupt detection by Interrupt Cycle and enabling unsupported pins having no effect.

Interrupt pin inputs are enabled by this field. Enable of unsupported interrupt pin is meaningless.

2.2.33.title: Slot Interrupt Status Register (Offset 0FCh)
2.2.33.abstract: The Slot Interrupt Status Register (offset 0FCh) provides logical OR status bits for interrupt and wakeup signals across up to 8 slots, enabling the host driver to identify which slot generated an interrupt when multiple slots share a signal; the register resets to 00h on power-on or software reset.

chunks.abstract: The Slot Interrupt Status Register (offset 0FCh) provides logical OR status bits for interrupt and wakeup signals across up to 8 slots, enabling the host driver to identify which slot generated an interrupt when multiple slots share a signal; the register resets to 00h on power-on or software reset.
chunks.raw: These status bits indicate the logical OR of Interrupt Signal and Wakeup Signal for each slot. A maximum of 8 slots can be defined. If one interrupt signal is associated with multiple slots, the Host Driver can know which interrupt is generated by reading these status bits. By a power on reset or by setting Software Reset For All, the interrupt signal shall be de-asserted and this status shall read 00h.

2.2.34.title: Host Controller Version Register (Offset 0FEh)
2.2.34.abstract: The Host Controller Version Register at offset 0FEh contains two fields: a reserved vendor version number field not for host driver use, and a specification version field where upper and lower 4-bits indicate the Host Controller specification version number.

chunks.abstract: The Host Controller Version Register at offset 0FEh contains two fields: a reserved vendor version number field not for host driver use, and a specification version field where upper and lower 4-bits indicate the Host Controller specification version number.
chunks.raw:
This status is reserved for the vendor version number. The Host Driver should not use this status.

This status indicates the Host Controller Spec. Version. The upper and lower 4-bits indicate the version.

3.title: SEQUENCE
3.abstract: This section specifies sequence flow charts for Host Driver interrupt handling, where "Wait for interrupts" indicates the driver waits for specified interrupt assertions with timeout checking. Double-boxed steps reference previously defined flows that may include interrupts.

chunks.abstract: This section specifies sequence flow charts for Host Driver interrupt handling, where "Wait for interrupts" indicates the driver waits for specified interrupt assertions with timeout checking. Double-boxed steps reference previously defined flows that may include interrupts.
chunks.raw:
This section defines basic sequence flow chart divided into several sub sequences.

"Wait for interrupts" is used in the flow chart. This means the Host Driver waits until specified interrupts are asserted. If already asserted, then fall through that step in the flow chart. Timeout checking shall be always required to detect no interrupt generated but this is not described in the flow chart.

This specification uses the double box like Figure 3-1, (the step (1) in Figure 3-5 and the step (5) in Figure 3-25), It means that the other flows, which already are shown, shall be performed. Therefore, the interrupt may be included in the other flows.

chunks.abstract: The abort command recovers from SD Bus errors, where SDIO abort (CMD52) always returns a response, but memory abort (CMD12) response depends on card state; if CMD12 fails to respond, the host driver must verify successful abort by checking for "tran" state using CMD13.
chunks.raw:
Implementation Note:
Abort command is used to recover from SD Bus error. SDIO transaction abort using CMD52 returns response but in the case of memory transaction abort using CMD12, response returns depending on the memory card state. If no response returns after issue CMD12, the Host Driver should check card state using CMD13. If the state is "tran" in the CURRENT_STATE, consider CMD12 is successful.

chunks.abstract: This specification describes an error recovery sequence for SD Bus operations, noting that alternative implementation methods exist using interrupts or polling. When commands cannot be issued due to SD Bus errors, the sequence returns a "Non-recoverable" status, requiring the Host System to power cycle the bus and reinitialize both controller and card.
chunks.raw:
Implementation Note:
The following sequence is one possible error recovery flow. There may be another methods, sometimes using interrupts or polling. It can be possible to use another flows, based on Host System requirements.

In these error recovery sequences, return statuses for the next sequence. When the Host Controller cannot issue the next command due to SD Bus error, the error recovery sequences return "Non-recoverable" status. In this case, the Host System may cut off power to the SD Bus, and then power on SD Bus and initialize both the Host Controller and the SD card again.

chunks.abstract: When Stop At Block Gap Request is set during the last block transfer, the Host Controller rejects it and completes the transaction normally without generating a Block Gap Event Interrupt. The driver must clear the Stop At Block Gap Request after Transfer Complete Interrupt if Block Gap Event status remains unset.
chunks.raw: If the Stop At Block Gap Request is set to 1 during the last block transfer, the Host Controller shall not accept the Stop At Block Gap Request and stops the transaction normally. The Block Gap Event Interrupt is not generated. When the Transfer Complete Interrupt is generated, and if the Block Gap Event status is not set to 1, the driver shall clear the Stop At Block Gap Request.

chunks.abstract: This specification describes the data transfer restart sequence, where setting Continue Request to 1 releases Read Wait, activates DAT Line and Read Transfer statuses, and auto-clears the request. Transfer completion is determined by data length, clearing active statuses and generating Transfer Complete Interrupt after all valid data is read.
chunks.raw:
To restart a stopped data transfer, set the Continue Request to 1. (The Stop At Block Gap Request shall be set to 0.)
After accepting the Continue Request,
(1) Release Read Wait (if the data block can accept the next data.)
(2) Set the DAT Line Active status and the Read Transfer Active status
(3) The Continue Request is automatically cleared by (2).
The end of the read transfer is specified by data length.
(1) Clear the DAT Line Active status and do not generate the Block Gap Event Interrupt.
(2) After all valid data has been read (No valid read data remains in the Host Controller), clear the Read Transfer Active status and generate the Transfer Complete Interrupt.

3.1.title: SD Card Detection
3.1.abstract: SD card detection is enabled by configuring four interrupt bits in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable and Signal Enable registers: setting Card Insertion Status Enable, Card Insertion Signal Enable, Card Removal Status Enable, and Card Removal Signal Enable bits to 1.

chunks.abstract: SD card detection is enabled by configuring four interrupt bits in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable and Signal Enable registers: setting Card Insertion Status Enable, Card Insertion Signal Enable, Card Removal Status Enable, and Card Removal Signal Enable bits to 1.
chunks.raw:
The flow chart for detecting a SD card is shown in Figure 3-2. Each step is executed as follows:

To enable interrupt for card detection, write 1 to the following bits:

Card Insertion Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register
Card Insertion Signal Enable in the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable register
Card Removal Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register
Card Removal Signal Enable in the Normal Interrupt Signal Enable register

3.2.1.title: SD Clock Supply Sequence

technical_terms: Base Clock Frequency For SD Clock

3.2.1.abstract: This specification defines the SD Clock supply sequence for SD cards, requiring clock frequency calculation from the Capabilities register, configuration of the Clock Control register's Internal Clock Enable and frequency settings, verification of clock stability, and finally enabling SD Clock before issuing commands or detecting interrupts.

chunks.abstract: This specification defines the SD Clock supply sequence for SD cards, requiring clock frequency calculation from the Capabilities register, configuration of the Clock Control register's Internal Clock Enable and frequency settings, verification of clock stability, and finally enabling SD Clock before issuing commands or detecting interrupts.
chunks.raw:
The sequence for supplying SD Clock to a SD card is described in Figure 3-3. The clock shall be supplied to the card before either of the following actions is taken.
a) Issuing a SD command
b) Detect an interrupt from a SD card in 4-bit mode.

(1) Calculate a divisor to determine SD Clock frequency by reading Base Clock Frequency For SD Clock in the Capabilities register. If Base Clock Frequency For SD Clock is 00 0000b, the Host System shall provide this information to the Host Driver by another method.
(2) Set Internal Clock Enable and SDCLK Frequency Select in the Clock Control register in accordance with the calculated result of step (1).
(3) Check Internal Clock Stable in the Clock Control register. Repeat this step until Clock Stable is 1.
(4) Set SD Clock Enable in the Clock Control register to 1. Then, the Host Controller starts to supply the SD Clock.

3.2.2.title: SD Clock Stop Sequence
3.2.2.abstract: The SD Clock Stop Sequence requires the Host Driver to set SD Clock Enable to 0 in the Clock Control register only when no SD transaction is active (Command Inhibit DAT and CMD bits are 0), after which the Host Controller ceases SD Clock supply.

chunks.abstract: The SD Clock Stop Sequence requires the Host Driver to set SD Clock Enable to 0 in the Clock Control register only when no SD transaction is active (Command Inhibit DAT and CMD bits are 0), after which the Host Controller ceases SD Clock supply.
chunks.raw:
The flow chart for stopping the SD Clock is shown in Figure 3-4. The Host Driver shall not stop the SD Clock when a SD transaction is occurring on the SD Bus -- namely, when either Command Inhibit (DAT) or Command Inhibit (CMD) in the Present State register is set to 1.

(1) Set SD Clock Enable in the Clock Control register to 0. Then, the Host Controller stops supplying the SD Clock.

3.2.3.title: SD Clock Frequency Change Sequence
3.2.3.abstract: The SD Clock frequency change sequence consists of two steps as detailed in Figure 3-5: step (1) addresses active clock conditions (omitted when SD Clock is off, see Section 3.2.2), and step (2) covers the frequency change procedure (see Section 3.2.1).

chunks.abstract: The SD Clock frequency change sequence consists of two steps as detailed in Figure 3-5: step (1) addresses active clock conditions (omitted when SD Clock is off, see Section 3.2.2), and step (2) covers the frequency change procedure (see Section 3.2.1).
chunks.raw: The sequence for changing SD Clock frequency is shown in Figure 3-5. When SD Clock is still off, step (1) is omitted. Please refer to Section 3.2.2 for details regarding step (1) and Section 3.2.1 for step (2).

3.3.title: SD Bus Power Control
3.3.abstract: Figure 3-6 describes the control sequence for managing power delivery to the SD Bus interface.

chunks.abstract: Figure 3-6 describes the control sequence for managing power delivery to the SD Bus interface.
chunks.raw: The sequence for controlling the SD Bus Power is described in Figure 3-6.

3.4.title: Changing Bus Width
3.4.abstract: This specification describes the five-step procedure for changing SD bus width, including masking card interrupts, disabling IENM in SDIO/combo cards via CMD52, switching card bus width using ACMD6 (SD Memory) or CCCR registers (SDIO), and configuring the Host Control register for 1-bit or 4-bit mode.

chunks.abstract: This specification describes the five-step procedure for changing SD bus width, including masking card interrupts, disabling IENM in SDIO/combo cards via CMD52, switching card bus width using ACMD6 (SD Memory) or CCCR registers (SDIO), and configuring the Host Control register for 1-bit or 4-bit mode.
chunks.raw:
The sequence for changing bit mode on SD Bus is shown in Figure 3-7.

(1) Set Card Interrupt Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register to 0 for masking incorrect interrupts that may occur while changing the bus width.
(2) In case of SD memory only card, go to step (4). In case of other card, go to step (3).
(3) Set "IENM" of the CCCR in a SDIO or SD combo card to 0 by CMD52. Please refer to Section 3.7.1 for how to generate CMD52.
(4) Change the bus width mode for a SD card. SD Memory Card bus width is changed by ACMD6 and SDIO card bus width is changed by setting Bus Width of Bus Interface Control register in CCCR.
(5) In case of changing to 4-bit mode, set Data Transfer Width to 1 in the Host Control 1 register. In another case (1-bit mode), set this bit to 0.

chunks.abstract: This specification details the final steps for changing bus width in SD cards: SD memory cards complete the process immediately, while SDIO and combo cards require enabling interrupt bits via CMD52 and status register configuration. Locked cards must be unlocked before any bus width changes.
chunks.raw:
(6) In case of SD memory only card, go to the 'End'. In case of other card, go to step (7).
(7) Set "IENM" of the CCCR in a SDIO or SD combo card to 1 by CMD52.
(8) Set Card Interrupt Status Enable in the Normal Interrupt Status Enable register to 1.

Note that if the card is locked, bus width cannot be changed. Unlock the card is required before changing bus width.

3.5.title: Timeout Setting on DAT Line
3.5.abstract: The Host Driver must configure DAT line timeout detection before SD transactions by: (1) calculating a divisor from the Capabilities register's Timeout Clock Frequency and Unit fields, and (2) programming the Timeout Control register's Data Timeout Counter Value accordingly.

chunks.abstract: The Host Driver must configure DAT line timeout detection before SD transactions by: (1) calculating a divisor from the Capabilities register's Timeout Clock Frequency and Unit fields, and (2) programming the Timeout Control register's Data Timeout Counter Value accordingly.
chunks.raw:
In order to detect timeout errors on DAT line, the Host Driver shall execute the following two steps before any SD transaction. For more information regarding SD transactions, refer to Section 3.7.2

(1) Calculate a divisor to detect timeout errors by reading Timeout Clock Frequency and Timeout Clock Unit in the Capabilities register. If Timeout Clock Frequency is 00 0000b, the Host System shall provide this information to the Host Driver by another method.
(2) Set Data Timeout Counter Value in the Timeout Control register in accordance with the value from step (1) above.

3.6.title: Card Initialization and Identification
3.6.abstract: This section presents the initialization and card identification sequence protocol for three SD Memory Card capacity types: Standard Capacity (SDSC), High Capacity (SDHC), and Extended Capacity (SDXC), as illustrated in Figure 3-9.

chunks.abstract: This section presents the initialization and card identification sequence protocol for three SD Memory Card capacity types: Standard Capacity (SDSC), High Capacity (SDHC), and Extended Capacity (SDXC), as illustrated in Figure 3-9.
chunks.raw: Figure 3-9 shows new initialization and card identification sequence for the Standard Capacity SD Memory Card (SDSC), the High Capacity SD Memory Card (SDHC) and the Extended Capacity SD Memory Card (SDXC).

chunks.abstract: When Stop At Block Gap Request is set during the final block transfer, the Host Controller ignores it and completes the transaction normally without generating a Block Gap Event Interrupt; the driver must then clear the Stop At Block Gap Request upon receiving the Transfer Complete Interrupt.
chunks.raw: If the Stop At Block Gap Request is set to 1 during the last block transfer, the Host Controller shall not accept the Stop At Block Gap Request and terminates the transaction normally. The Block Gap Event Interrupt is not generated. When the Transfer Complete Interrupt is generated, and if the Block Gap Event Interrupt Status is not set to 1, the driver shall clear the Stop At Block Gap Request.

chunks.abstract: This specification defines the protocol for resuming stopped data transfers by setting Continue Request to 1, which activates DAT Line and Write Transfer statuses. Transfer completion is determined by data length, clearing Write Transfer Active status and generating Transfer Complete Interrupt after busy signal release.
chunks.raw:
To restart a stopped data transfer, set the Continue Request to 1. (Stop At Block Gap Request shall be set to 0.)

After accepting the Continue Request:
(1) Set the DAT Line Active status and the Write Transfer Active Status
(2) The Continue Request is automatically cleared by (1).

The end of transfer is specified by data length.
(1) Clear the Write Transfer Active Status, and do not generate the Block Gap Event Interrupt
(2) After the busy signal is released, clear the DAT Line Active status and generates the Transfer Complete Interrupt.

3.6.1.title: Signal Voltage Switch Procedure
3.6.1.abstract: The Signal Voltage Switch Procedure defines the protocol for transitioning SD card interface voltage levels between 3.3V and 1.8V signaling modes to enable higher-speed data transfer rates while maintaining backward compatibility with legacy devices.

chunks.abstract: The Signal Voltage Switch Procedure defines the protocol for transitioning SD card interface voltage levels between 3.3V and 1.8V signaling modes to enable higher-speed data transfer rates while maintaining backward compatibility with legacy devices.
chunks.raw: Signal Voltage Switch Procedure

chunks.abstract: This specification defines the SD card signal voltage switch procedure from 3.3V to 1.8V, initiated by CMD11 after S18A flag detection. The 12-step sequence includes stopping the SD clock, verifying DAT line levels (0000b then 1111b), enabling the 1.8V regulator with specific timing delays, and error handling with initialization retry.
chunks.raw:
(1) If S18A of CMD5 or S18A of ACMD41 is set to 1, signal voltage switch is performed according to the following steps. Otherwise, exits from this procedure.
(2) Issue CMD11.
(3) Check response and if an error is detected, go to step (12)
(4) Stop providing SD clock to the card.
(5) Check DAT[3:0] level. If the level is 0000b, the card is ready to start voltage switch sequence. Otherwise, go to (12) to quit the sequence.
(6) Set 1.8V Signal Enable in the Host Control 2 register.
(7) Wait 5ms. 1.8V voltage regulator shall be stable within this period.
(8) If 1.8V Signal Enable is cleared by Host Controller, go to step (12).
(9) Provide SD Clock to the card again.
(10) Wait 1ms.
(11) Check DAT[3:0] level. If the level is 1111b, switch to 1.8V signal level is completed successfully. Otherwise, go to (12).
(12) If an error occurs during voltage switch procedure, stop providing the power to the card. In this case, Host Driver should retry initialization procedure by setting S18R to 0 at step (7) and (21) in Figure 3-9.

3.7.title: SD Transaction Generation
3.7.abstract: This specification defines the 9-step procedure for SD card transaction generation, including configuring block size/count registers, setting argument and transfer mode parameters, issuing commands via the Command register, handling completion interrupts, and reading responses before proceeding to write (step 10) or read (step 14) operations.

chunks.abstract: This specification defines the 9-step procedure for SD card transaction generation, including configuring block size/count registers, setting argument and transfer mode parameters, issuing commands via the Command register, handling completion interrupts, and reading responses before proceeding to write (step 10) or read (step 14) operations.
chunks.raw:
(1) Set the value corresponding to the executed data byte length of one block to Block Size register.
(2) Set the value corresponding to the executed data block count to Block Count register in accordance with Table 2-8.
(3) Set the argument value to Argument 1 register.
(4) Set the value to the Transfer Mode register. The host driver determines Multi / Single Block Select, Block Count Enable, Data Transfer Direction, Auto CMD12 Enable and DMA Enable. Multi / Single Block Select and Block Count Enable are determined according to Table 2-8.
(5) Set the value to Command register.
Note: When writing the upper byte [3] of Command register, SD command is issued.
(6) Then, wait for the Command Complete Interrupt.
(7) Write 1 to the Command Complete in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(8) Read Response register and get necessary information of the issued command.
(9) In the case where this sequence is for write to a card, go to step (10). In case of read from a card, go to step (14).

chunks.abstract: This specification details the SD card transaction generation procedure, including interrupt-driven buffer write/read operations through the Buffer Data Port register, block transfer handling (single, multiple, or infinite), and transaction completion steps involving Normal Interrupt Status register manipulation and abort sequence execution.
chunks.raw:
(10) Then wait for Buffer Write Ready Interrupt.
(11) Write 1 to the Buffer Write Ready in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(12) Write block data (in according to the number of bytes specified at the step (1)) to Buffer Data Port register.
(13) Repeat until all blocks are sent and then go to step (18).
(14) Then wait for the Buffer Read Ready Interrupt.
(15) Write 1 to the Buffer Read Ready in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(16) Read block data (in according to the number of bytes specified at the step (1)) from the Buffer Data Port register.
(17) Repeat until all blocks are received and then go to step (18).
(18) If this sequence is for Single or Multiple Block Transfer, go to step (19). In case of Infinite Block Transfer, go to step (21).
(19) Wait for Transfer Complete Interrupt.
(20) Write 1 to the Transfer Complete in the Normal Interrupt Status register for clearing this bit.
(21) Perform the sequence for Abort Transaction in accordance with Section 3.8.
Note: Step (1) and Step (2) can be executed at same time. Step (4) and Step (5) can be executed at same time.

chunks.abstract: This specification defines SD transaction generation sequences, categorizing them into three types based on DAT line usage: no DAT line usage, DAT line for busy signals only, and DAT line for data transfer, with the first two grouped as non-data transactions and the third as data transactions.
chunks.raw:
This section describes the sequences how to generate and control various kinds of SD transactions. SD transactions are classified into three cases:
(1) Transactions that do not use the DAT line.
(2) Transactions that use the DAT line only for the busy signal.
(3) Transactions that use the DAT line for transferring data.

In this specification the first and the second case's transactions are classified as "Transaction Control without Data Transfer using DAT Line", the third case's transaction is classified as "Transaction Control with Data Transfer using DAT Line".
Refer to the latest SD Physical Layer Specification and SDIO Specification for more detail about SD commands specification.

3.7.1.1.title: The Sequence to Issue a SD Command
3.7.1.1.abstract: This section details the procedural sequence required to issue commands to an SD (Secure Digital) card, specifying the exact steps and timing for proper SD command transmission and execution.

chunks.abstract: This specification defines a seven-step sequence for issuing SD commands: verify Command Inhibit (CMD) flag is cleared, check for busy signal and abort command conditions, verify Command Inhibit (DAT) if needed, write command argument to Argument 1 register, set Command register to trigger command execution, then perform command completion sequence.
chunks.raw:
(1) Check Command Inhibit (CMD) in the Present State register. Repeat this step until Command Inhibit (CMD) is 0. That is, when Command Inhibit (CMD) is 1, the Host Driver shall not issue a SD Command.
(2) If the Host Driver issues a SD Command with busy signal, go to step (3). If without busy signal, go to step (5).
(3) If the Host Driver issues an abort command, go to step (5). In the case of no abort command, go to step (4).
(4) Check Command Inhibit (DAT) in the Present State register. Repeat this step until Command Inhibit (DAT) is set to 0.
(5) Set the value of command argument to the Argument 1 register.
(6) Set the Command register.
Note: Writing the upper byte [3] in the Command register causes the host controller to issue a SD command to the SD card.
(7) Perform Command Completion Sequence in accordance with 3.7.1.2.
